Cuando te registras en un servicio, el s: When you sign up to a service, the server should not store your password. If it stores it and the database is stolen, the thief has your password, and probably your email one too, because people reuse them. What it stores is its hash: when you log in, it hashes what you type and compares. That seems to settle it. It does not settle it entirely, and the difference between doing it well and doing it badly is a few hours against a few centuries.

The idea is to use a deliberately slow hash: instead of one SHA-256, a hundred thousand SHA-256s chained, or better, a function that also needs a lot of memory, so that graphics cards, which have little of it per core, lose their advantage. For the user, logging in takes a tenth of a second. For the attacker, each candidate costs a hundred thousand times more.
Las fugas lo demuestran. En 2012 se filt: The leaks prove it. In 2012, 6.5 million hashes from a professional network were leaked, SHA-1 with no salt: 90 % was broken in days. In 2009 a social network stored 32 million passwords in the clear, and that list is today the starting dictionary of any attacker. In 2013 a software company encrypted 150 million with 3DES in ECB mode, and repeated passwords showed up as repeated ciphertexts. Today's guidelines ask for Argon2, scrypt or bcrypt with a cost tuned to a tenth of a second, and password managers and passwordless passkeys, which you will see at the end of the block, make none of this necessary.

A dictionary of $10^{10}$ candidates, at $10^{10}$ hashes per second, is run through in one second. With $10^5$ iterations, in $10^5$ seconds: more than a day per user. And with a million salted users, three thousand years.

The number of iterations is raised over the years, as machines improve: that is the cost factor, and the modern functions, bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2, carry it written into the hash itself.
Un hash no se invierte, pero una contras: A hash is not inverted, but a password is not just any message: it is short and predictable. With the stolen database, the attacker needs to invert nothing. A graphics card does ten billion SHA-256s per second: the whole dictionary in a fraction of a second, and every combination of eight lower-case letters in twenty seconds.
